title: Pay Our Homeland Defenders Act
official_title: Making appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Passed the House and was received in the Senate. Sponsored by Rep. Ciscomani (R-AZ). It pairs full-year Homeland Security funding with provisions to cover a funding lapse and pay employees, which creates pressure to act, but full-year DHS appropriations are contentious over immigration enforcement and it still needs 60 votes in the Senate.
summary: Provides full-year fiscal year 2026 funding for the Department of Homeland Security — including Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the TSA — and, in a second division, retroactively covers a lapse in appropriations that began around February 13, 2026 and makes the pay and benefits of affected employees available, authorizing back pay for the lapse period (forward funding comes from the full-year appropriations in the first division, not this one).
brief: Full-year DHS funding for FY2026 plus a division that covers a February 2026 funding lapse and pays affected employees.

top_lines.headline: Full-Year Homeland Security Funding
subs: Funds Customs and Border Protection operations at $17.73B and ICE operations at $10.04B
Funds the Transportation Security Administration at $10.64B (about $7.6B from the general fund after security fees)

Funds the Federal Emergency Management Agency, including the $26.37B Disaster Relief Fund — the bill's single largest account — plus $3.84B in Federal Assistance grants and $1.67B for operations and support
Covers the Department through the end of fiscal year 2026

top_lines.headline: Covers a Funding Lapse and Back Pay
subs: Treats the period of the appropriations lapse that began around February 13, 2026 as covered by the FY2026 continuing resolution
Makes employee pay, allowances, and benefits available for payment under the Antideficiency Act's exception
Ratifies obligations incurred during the lapse to protect life and property

top_lines.headline: Enforcement Funding and Controls
subs: Authorizes CBP to buy up to 7,500 police-type vehicles and ICE up to 3,790
Earmarks ICE funds for forced-child-labor enforcement, intellectual-property investigations, and child-rescue apprenticeships
Requires congressional notification before larger reprogrammings (over $5M or 10%) and most fund transfers

sections.label: Title II — Customs and Border Protection

items.main: Funds CBP operations and procurement for fiscal year 2026.
items.detail: Appropriates $17.73B for CBP operations and support — covering air and marine support, transportation of unaccompanied minors, and up to 7,500 police-type vehicles (6,500 for replacement) — with $550M available through September 30, 2027, plus $222.89M for procurement, construction, and improvements.

sections.label: Title II — Immigration and Customs Enforcement

items.main: Funds ICE operations and sets aside amounts for specific enforcement priorities.
items.detail: Appropriates $10.04B for ICE operations and support (including up to 3,790 police-type vehicles), of which Homeland Security Investigations amounts include not less than $6M for enforcing laws against forced child labor, not less than $15M for intellectual-property-rights investigations, and $3M for child-rescue apprenticeships, plus $5M for procurement, construction, and improvements.

items.main: Funds the TSA, offset by aviation security fees.
items.detail: Appropriates $10.64B for TSA operations and support, with security service fees credited as offsetting collections so that the net general-fund appropriation is estimated at not more than $7.61B for fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Sets limits and notification requirements on moving DHS funds between purposes.
items.detail: Bars reprogrammings that create or eliminate programs, augment a program by more than $5M or 10 percent, or cut a program or personnel by 10 percent or more, unless the Appropriations Committees are notified 30 days in advance, and limits transfers between appropriations to 5 percent (and no more than a 10 percent increase to any account).

sections.label: Section 1001 — Coverage of the Appropriations Lapse

items.main: Retroactively treats a funding lapse as covered by the FY2026 continuing resolution.
items.detail: Provides that, for purposes of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 (division A of Public Law 119-37), the time covered includes the period beginning on or about February 13, 2026 during which a lapse in appropriations occurred.

items.main: Makes pay, allowances, and benefits available to affected employees.
items.detail: Provides that amounts under the FY2026 continuing resolution and the DHS appropriations in division A for personnel pay, allowances, and benefits are available for payments under the Antideficiency Act exception (31 U.S.C. 1341(c)), and that such payments shall be made.

items.main: Ratifies obligations incurred during the lapse.
items.detail: Ratifies and approves obligations incurred in anticipation of the FY2026 continuing resolution and division A for maintaining the essential level of activity to protect life and property and to bring about an orderly termination of government functions, if otherwise in accord with the applicable Act.

underreported.summary: Two non-DHS riders are attached to the bill: a $140M FAA appropriation funding a 3.8% pay raise for air traffic controllers, and $30M in additional funding for the Supreme Court.
underreported.why_unreported: Non-germane appropriations riders tucked into a departmental funding bill; not reflected in the bill's title or the DHS-focused sections.
